Where it began

Ian Healy was born on 30 April 1964 in Spring Hill, a suburb of Brisbane. When he was a boy his family moved north to the small town of Biloela, where he played every sport going, from basketball to rugby league. Rod Marsh was his hero, and Marsh was why he took up the gloves.

In Biloela he was soon playing alongside grown men, which sped up his learning. Back in Brisbane he joined Northern Suburbs and made his first-class debut for Queensland in 1986–87. His brother Ken also played for Queensland, in a single Sheffield Shield match.

The player

After only six first-class games, he was picked for Australia's tour of Pakistan in 1988. It came as a big surprise, not least to Healy. The selectors stuck with him, and he repaid them many times over across 119 Tests up to 1999.

He held 366 catches and made 29 stumpings, and he scored 4,356 runs at 27.40 with four hundreds and 22 fifties. His first century, 102 not out at Old Trafford in 1993, came in a stand with Steve Waugh. His highest score was 161 not out. In October 1998 at Rawalpindi he passed his old hero Marsh's world record of 355 Test dismissals, and he finished with 395.

What made him special

Keeping to Shane Warne is one of the hardest jobs in cricket, and Healy made it look natural. In his first 39 Tests he made two stumpings. In 14 Tests between 1992 and 1993, with Warne bowling, he made ten. He learned to read every variation the leg-spinner had.

He was also the loudest voice in the field. Stump microphones carried his steady encouragement to the bowlers, Warne above all, into living rooms across the country. And he was a good batsman when it mattered most. He top-scored with 90 in a Test at Chennai.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year in 1994, and when the Australian Cricket Board picked its team of the 20th century, he was the man behind the stumps. Two halls of fame followed: Sport Australia's in 2004, and Australian cricket's own in 2008.

He became a cricket commentator in 1999, presented sport on Nine News Queensland and, from 2020, co-hosted a breakfast radio show in Queensland. His niece Alyssa Healy took up the gloves too, keeping wicket for Australia's women.

And finally

A Brisbane ground carries his name, and in March 2021 the Ian Healy Oval was approved for first-class cricket. It is a fitting tribute, and probably the only patch of grass in Queensland he never had to dive across.
